items.prompt: What's the difference between authentication and authorization?
choices: They're the same underlying check, just described using two different pieces of industry terminology
Authentication answers 'who are you'; authorization answers 'what are you allowed to do' — a system can get the first completely right while failing the second
Authentication is the check reserved for admin accounts, while authorization is the equivalent check used for regular users
Authorization always runs and completes before authentication ever gets a chance to verify who's making the request
items.explanation: These are genuinely separate questions — the invoice endpoint proved a system can correctly authenticate a user while still failing to authorize their specific request.
items.reference:

Valid session?Authentication
Owns this resource?Authorization

Why: the invoice endpoint got authentication right and skipped authorization entirely.
items.learnMore:
Two separate gates

Treating 'logged in' as sufficient proof of 'allowed to see this' is one of the most common real-world authorization mistakes, precisely because the two checks feel related but are structurally independent.

Common mistake

Writing `if (isLoggedIn)` and treating that as a complete access check.

items.prompt: What is the name for the specific vulnerability class the invoice incident represents?
choices: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) — injecting a script that runs in another user's browser session
Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR)
SQL Injection — manipulating a query's structure by supplying unexpected input through a form field
Denial of Service — overwhelming the endpoint with enough traffic that legitimate requests can't get through
items.explanation: IDOR describes exactly this pattern: an object (here, an invoice) is referenced directly by an ID the client controls, with no check that the requester should have access to that specific object.
items.reference:
IDOR — Insecure Direct Object Reference

Checking login status but not resource ownership.

Why: it's common enough to have a standard name because it's an easy check to accidentally omit.
items.learnMore:
A common, well-known pattern

IDOR is one of the most frequently reported real-world web vulnerabilities specifically because it's easy to write an endpoint that 'obviously' requires login and never separately verify resource ownership.

Common mistake

Assuming a well-tested, working endpoint can't have this bug simply because it requires login.

items.prompt: Why is IDOR common enough to have a standard, well-known name?
choices: Because it only ever happens in poorly written code produced by genuinely inexperienced developers
Because it's easy to write an endpoint that requires login and never separately verify that the specific resource belongs to the requester
Because it's actually a deliberate, intentional design choice baked into most production systems on purpose
It isn't actually common at all in real codebases — this is simply a misconception about how often it occurs
items.explanation: The pattern recurs across many codebases and skill levels precisely because the missing check is easy to overlook — requiring login FEELS like it should be sufficient, which is the trap.

items.prompt: What is an "authorization model"?
choices: A UML diagram documenting the login system's sequence of calls between client and server
A systematic answer to 'what determines whether this request should succeed' — like RBAC or ABAC
A minimum password strength and complexity requirement enforced at account creation time
A synonym security teams use interchangeably for encryption at rest and in transit
items.explanation: An authorization model is the systematic rule set (like RBAC or ABAC) that determines access decisions — not a diagram, password policy, or encryption scheme.
items.reference:
RBAC — permissions attached to a role

ABAC — permissions computed from user/resource/context attributes

Why: two common, complementary approaches to answering 'should this request succeed.'
items.learnMore:
A systematic rule set

Rather than ad-hoc checks scattered through code, an authorization model gives a consistent, auditable framework for deciding access — which is exactly what the invoice endpoint lacked.

Common mistake

Writing ad-hoc, inconsistent access checks per endpoint instead of applying a consistent model.

Resource-Based Access Control and Auth-Based Access Control, two terms sometimes used interchangeably
Rule-Based Access Control and Account-Based Access Control, a pairing used in some legacy systems
items.explanation: RBAC ties permissions to a role; ABAC computes access from attributes of the user, resource, and context.

ABAC — permissions computed from user/resource/context attributes

items.prompt: Can a correctly-implemented RBAC check alone fix the invoice IDOR bug?
choices: Yes — RBAC can express any authorization rule at all, given a sufficiently detailed role definition
No — 'is this role allowed to view invoices' is true regardless of WHICH invoice, so RBAC alone can never express per-resource ownership
Yes, but only once the role hierarchy becomes complex enough to encode individual resource ownership
No, because RBAC as a model simply doesn't apply to invoices or other billing-related resources
items.explanation: This is L1/L2's central technical point — RBAC answers a role-level question that's structurally incapable of expressing 'this specific resource belongs to this specific user.'
items.reference:
QuestionModel
Can a billing-viewer view invoices at all?RBAC
Can THIS billing-viewer view THIS invoice?ABAC-style

Why: roles don't carry per-resource identity — a role is the same regardless of which invoice is requested.
items.learnMore:
Why role checks structurally can't express ownership

A role is a property of the user alone — it has no way to reference which specific resource is being requested, so no role-only rule can ever encode 'this resource, this user' the way an attribute comparison can.

Common mistake

Believing a fine-grained enough role hierarchy could eventually express per-resource ownership — it structurally cannot, no matter how many roles are added.

items.prompt: Per L2's flowchart, in what order does a well-designed system check authentication, role permission, and resource ownership?
choices: Resource ownership first, then role-level permission, then authentication last of all
Authentication first, then role-level (RBAC) permission, then resource-level (ABAC-style) ownership
All three checks run simultaneously in parallel, with no defined order between them
Role-level permission first, then authentication, then resource ownership last
items.explanation: L2's flowchart shows this exact sequence — each check gates the next, and failing any one stops the request before the next check runs.
items.reference:
1. Valid session? (401 if no)

2. Role allowed for this action? (403 if no)

3. Resource belongs to this actor? (403 if no)

Why: the invoice bug's gap was specifically between steps 2 and 3.
items.learnMore:
A gated sequence

Each check exists specifically to catch a different failure mode — skipping any one reopens exactly that failure mode, regardless of how well the other checks are implemented.

Common mistake

Assuming the checks are redundant with each other rather than each catching a distinct class of bug.

items.prompt: In L2's RBAC example, does a 'billing-viewer' role have the 'refund-invoice' permission?
choices: Yes, a billing-viewer role is granted refund-invoice as part of its default permission set
No — only 'billing-admin' has refund-invoice in the example permission set
It depends entirely on which specific invoice is being targeted by the refund request
RBAC as a model doesn't define specific, named permissions on a per-role basis at all
items.explanation: L2's example explicitly lists billing-viewer's permissions as view-invoice and view-billing-history only — refund-invoice belongs to billing-admin.
items.reference:
billing-viewer: [view-invoice, view-billing-history]

billing-admin: [view-invoice, view-billing-history, edit-invoice, refund-invoice]

Why: RBAC ties specific permissions to specific role names.
items.learnMore:
Roles as permission buckets

A role is just a named collection of permissions — checking access under RBAC is checking whether the user's role's permission list includes the required permission.

Common mistake

Assuming any authenticated user with SOME role automatically has every permission a more privileged role would have.

By checking whether the user's assigned role's permission list includes the permission required for the requested action
By checking whether the requesting user has been active at all within the last five minutes
By checking the total byte size of the incoming request's payload against a configured limit
items.explanation: This is the core RBAC mechanism — the user's role determines their permission set, and the check verifies the required permission is in that set.

items.prompt: In L2's ABAC rule (`user.id == invoice.ownerId OR user.role == 'billing-admin'`), what two kinds of values does the comparison use?
choices: Two separate attributes belonging to the user alone, with nothing drawn from the resource
An attribute of the user and an attribute of the resource being requested
Two separate attributes belonging to the resource alone, with nothing drawn from the user
The current server's system timestamp compared against the size of the incoming request
items.explanation: ABAC's defining feature is comparing attributes across different entities — here, an attribute of the requesting user (`user.id`) against an attribute of the specific resource (`invoice.ownerId`).
items.reference:
ALLOW view-invoice IF user.id == invoice.ownerId OR user.role == "billing-admin"

Why: this comparison is exactly the check the vulnerable endpoint was missing.
items.learnMore:
Cross-entity comparison

ABAC's power comes specifically from comparing attributes ACROSS entities (user vs. resource), which is structurally different from RBAC's single-entity (user's role) lookup.

Common mistake

Writing an 'ABAC-style' check that only inspects user attributes, missing the resource-side comparison that makes it meaningful.

Yes — the rule's OR clause explicitly grants access to any billing-admin regardless of ownership
Only if they also happen to independently own the specific invoice being requested
The rule as written simply doesn't address this particular case either way
items.explanation: The OR clause in the ABAC rule explicitly carves out broader access for billing-admin, independent of the ownership match.
items.reference:
ALLOW view-invoice IF user.id == invoice.ownerId OR user.role == "billing-admin"

Why: this comparison is exactly the check the vulnerable endpoint was missing.

items.prompt: Does fixing the invoice bug mean abandoning RBAC entirely in favor of ABAC?
choices: Yes — ABAC should fully replace RBAC everywhere once resource-level checks are introduced
No — most real systems combine both, since they answer complementary questions (role-level gating and resource-level ownership)
Yes, RBAC is considered fully deprecated and unnecessary in any modern authorization system
No, ABAC-style ownership checks should never be used alongside an existing RBAC layer
items.explanation: L2 is explicit that both checks are needed together — RBAC gates whether the kind of action is possible at all, ABAC-style checks gate the specific resource.
items.reference:
RBAC: is this kind of action allowed for this role?

ABAC-style: does this resource belong to this actor?

Both required.

Why: removing either check reopens a hole.
items.learnMore:
Complementary, not competing

RBAC and ABAC aren't rival approaches to pick one over the other — they typically compose, each catching a different class of bug the other can't.

Common mistake

Treating the choice between RBAC and ABAC as either/or, rather than recognizing most systems need both.

items.prompt: What happens if the fixed invoice endpoint used ONLY the ABAC-style ownership check, with no RBAC gating at all?

items.prompt: Implement `abacAllowsViewInvoice(user, invoice)` — return `true` if `invoice.ownerId === user.id`, OR if `user.role === 'billing-admin'`. Otherwise `false`.

tests.description: admin is allowed regardless of ownership

items.explanation: This is L2/L3's exact ABAC rule — comparing an attribute of the user against an attribute of the resource, plus the admin carve-out, exactly matching the incident's fix.

items.prompt: Implement `abacAllowsViewInvoice(user, invoice)` (same rules). Verify it correctly reproduces the incident: it must deny user 42 viewing user 7's invoice, and allow user 7 viewing their own.
items.explanation: Reproducing L1's exact incident with this function confirms it's the precise missing check that would have prevented the vulnerability from ever shipping.

items.prompt: Implement `abacAllowsViewInvoice(user, invoice)` (same rules). Confirm the function handles equal and non-equal numeric IDs correctly.

tests.description: numeric ids compare correctly when equal
numeric ids compare correctly when different

items.explanation: Strict equality between the two numeric IDs is exactly the comparison this check needs — this is the simplest possible correct implementation of the ownership rule.

items.prompt: Implement `canAccessInvoice(user, invoice)` by composing `rbacAllows` and `abacAllowsViewInvoice` (both provided) — access requires BOTH the role permission for 'view-invoice' AND the ownership/admin check to pass.

tests.description: owner with correct role is allowed
non-owner is denied even with the right role
role with no view-invoice permission is denied even if somehow the owner

items.explanation: This is L2's 'combine both' diagram made concrete — requiring both checks to pass together, catching both a wrong role AND a wrong resource, matching exactly the composed defense the unit describes.

items.prompt: Implement `canAccessInvoice(user, invoice)` (same composition). Verify it correctly denies access for a role with no invoice-viewing permission at all, even though they happen to be the owner (edge case demonstrating why RBAC alone isn't skippable).

tests.description: billing-admin with no ownership still allowed

items.explanation: A suspended user owning their old invoice is still correctly denied because RBAC gates them out first — demonstrating why ABAC alone (ownership only) isn't sufficient either, exactly as L2 explains.

items.prompt: Implement `abacAllowsViewTeamInvoice(user, invoice, userTeamIds)` from L3's extension — return `true` if `userTeamIds` includes `invoice.teamId`, OR if `user.role === 'billing-admin'`.
items.explanation: This generalizes the single-owner ABAC pattern to a membership check — same attribute-of-user-vs-attribute-of-resource shape, just comparing team membership instead of a single ID match, exactly as L3's extension describes.

items.prompt: Implement `abacAllowsViewTeamInvoice(user, invoice, userTeamIds)` (same rules). Verify a user on MULTIPLE teams is granted access if ANY of their teams matches the invoice's team.

tests.description: user on 3 teams, invoice matches the 2nd

items.explanation: Array membership (`.includes`) naturally handles the multi-team case — the user is granted access if any single team membership matches, without needing special-case logic for how many teams they belong to.

items.prompt: Implement `abacAllowsViewTeamInvoice(user, invoice, userTeamIds)` (same rules). Verify a billing-admin is allowed even with an empty `userTeamIds` list, while a non-admin with an empty list is denied.

tests.description: admin allowed with no team memberships at all
non-admin with no teams is denied

items.explanation: The admin carve-out (OR clause) is independent of team membership entirely — this confirms the two conditions are evaluated separately, not as a combined single check.
